consensus_summary: All four blinded responses converge on a christological/eucharistic core: bread primarily symbolizes Jesus Christ himself as the Bread of Life and his body given in the Lord's Supper (John 6; Matt 26:26; 1 Cor 11), grounded in the wider motif of God's life-giving provision (manna). The word-of-God/spiritual-nourishment reading (Deut 8:3; Matt 4:4) appears in every response, but only as a common secondary alternative, sometimes folded into the christological sense.
book_summary: The book identifies bread simply and solely as 'the word of God,' citing Deuteronomy 8:3 and Matthew 4:4 ('man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God'), with a cross-reference to a chapter on orphans, widows, and the fatherless. No christological or eucharistic identification is offered.
consensus_core_identification: Bread = Christ himself — the Bread of Life and his body given for believers, concentrated in the Eucharist/Lord's Supper.
book_core_identification: Bread = the word of God (divine speech/Scripture as spiritual sustenance).
boundary_disagreement: The consensus treats the word-of-God sense as one common layer of a multivalent symbol whose center is Christ/Eucharist; the book collapses the symbol to that single layer, implicitly excluding the Bread of Life discourse, the Last Supper institution words, manna typology of Christ, fellowship/one-loaf, and unleavened-bread senses that the consensus regards as central or common.
material_contradiction: As competing identifications of the symbol's primary referent, 'bread is Christ's body/Christ himself' and 'bread is the word of God' cannot both be the core meaning in the same sense. Accepting the book's flat, exclusive identification requires displacing the consensus's christological-eucharistic core rather than merely trimming its boundary. (They are theologically relatable — Christ as the Logos — but the book draws no such bridge.)
rationale: The book's referent is present in every consensus response, but only as a secondary alternative; the book elevates it to the sole meaning while omitting the dominant Christ/Eucharist identification entirely. This is replacement of the central referent, not a boundary refinement within the same core, so DIVERGENT rather than REFINED. It is not NOVEL because the word-of-God reading is a well-attested listed alternative. Extensionally, the book's cases (Deut 8:3; Matt 4:4 and kindred word-as-nourishment texts) are a subset of the passages the consensus already covers under its broader multivalent treatment.
strongest_objection: One could argue REFINED: the consensus's broadest category is 'God-given spiritual nourishment,' and the book merely narrows within that category to the word of God — a sense every response lists as common, and one the notes in Response A even say is often folded into the christological reading (Christ as the Word). Additionally, the cited verses themselves set bread in contrast to the word ('not by bread alone'), so the equation bread=word is derivative; a defender would say the analogy of nourishment underwrites it, keeping the book within the consensus's own recognized range.
